two-sum: Try using extra memory to speed up lookup: map each value to its index as you scan.
For each index i, the complement you need is target minus nums[i]. Have you seen it already?
A hash map from number to index lets you test the complement in O(1) time per element.
reverse-string: Two pointers: one at the start, one at the end; swap and move inward.
You can do this in place with O(1) extra space if the string is mutable.
Stop when the left index meets or crosses the right index.
valid-parentheses: Track opening symbols in order; a closing symbol must match the most recent unmatched opener.
A stack naturally models last-opened-first-closed structure.
If the stack is empty when you need to pop, or non-empty at the end, the string is invalid.
best-time-to-buy-and-sell-stock: For each day as a sell day, the best buy is the minimum price seen before that day.
One pass: keep running minimum price and best profit so far.
You only need one transaction, so compare every price against the min so far.
merge-two-sorted-lists: Compare heads of both lists repeatedly and append the smaller node.
A dummy head node simplifies appending without special cases.
When one list empties, attach the remainder of the other list.
missing-number: The sum 0..n is n(n+1)/2; subtract the sum of the array to find the missing value.
XOR every index and every value; duplicates cancel and the missing number remains.
Sorting or a boolean array works but uses more time or space.
contains-duplicate: A set records values you have seen; duplicate if insert fails.
Sorting adjacent equal elements also reveals duplicates.
Prefer O(n) time with a hash set when memory allows.
valid-palindrome: Filter to alphanumeric characters, then compare from both ends.
Compare case-insensitively after normalizing each character.
maximum-subarray: Kadane: extend a segment while its sum helps; reset when sum drops below zero.
At each position, best ending here is max(nums[i], prevSum + nums[i]).
Track global maximum across all ending positions.
climbing-stairs: Ways to step n equals ways to (n-1) plus ways to (n-2).
This is the Fibonacci sequence with base cases for n=1 and n=2.
Iterative DP uses O(1) space; matrix exponentiation is possible for huge n.
linked-list-cycle: Slow and fast pointers: if there is a cycle, fast will eventually meet slow.
If fast reaches null, there is no cycle.
Move fast two steps per iteration and slow one step.
invert-binary-tree: Swap left and right children at each node, then recurse (or use a queue).
Handle null children explicitly when swapping.
longest-substring-without-repeating-char: Sliding window: expand when the character is new, shrink from the left when it repeats.
A map stores last index of each character in the current window.
Update max length whenever the window is valid.
3sum: Sort first, then fix one index and use two pointers for the rest.
Skip duplicate values after sorting to avoid duplicate triplets.
Target for two-sum becomes zero minus the fixed element.
product-of-array-except-self: Prefix products of all elements to the left, suffix products to the right.
Answer at i is prefix[i-1] times suffix[i+1].
Can do O(1) extra space by output array as prefix storage, then multiply by suffix pass.
number-of-islands: DFS or BFS from each unvisited land cell; mark visited cells as water or use a visited set.
Boundary check: stay inside the grid.
course-schedule: Cycle in a directed graph means impossible schedule; topological sort detects it.
Compute indegree; repeatedly remove nodes with indegree zero.
If you process all n nodes, no cycle; otherwise a cycle exists.
coin-change: DP: minCoins(amount) = 1 + min over coins of minCoins(amount - coin).
Base case: amount zero needs zero coins; unreachable amounts stay infinity.
Bottom-up iteration avoids stack depth issues.
top-k-frequent-elements: Count frequencies with a hash map, then bucket by frequency or use a heap.
Bucket sort: index is frequency; list of numbers with that count.
Min-heap of size k on (frequency, value) pairs also works.
lowest-common-ancestor-of-a-binary-searc: If both values are smaller than root, LCA is in the left subtree.
If both are larger, LCA is in the right subtree.
Otherwise the current node splits them and is the LCA.
implement-trie-prefix-tree: Each node holds a map of char to child node and an end-of-word flag.
Insert walks or creates path; search follows path; prefix checks same path exists.
26 children or a map scales to any alphabet size.
container-with-most-water: Two pointers at both ends; area is width times min of the two heights.
Move the pointer with the smaller height inward to possibly increase area.
Greedy works because shorter side limits the area.
search-in-rotated-sorted-array: Binary search: at least one half is normally sorted.
Compare mid with target and endpoints to decide which half is safe.
Handle duplicates by shrinking bounds when nums[left] equals nums[mid].
group-anagrams: Sort characters of each string to get a canonical key, or count letters.
Hash map from key to list of strings.
Counting array of length 26 works for lowercase English letters.
rotate-image: Transpose the matrix, then reverse each row (or reverse layers in place).
Rotate four cells at a time in layers from outside to inside.
validate-binary-search-tree: Each node must lie within (min, max) bounds inherited from ancestors.
Inorder traversal of a valid BST yields strictly increasing values.
Pass allowed min and max down the recursion.
binary-tree-level-order-traversal: BFS with a queue; process level by level using level size.
Alternate: DFS with depth index appending to lists.
Track current level count before dequeuing children.
rotting-oranges: Multi-source BFS from all rotten cells at minute zero.
Each round spreads to fresh neighbors in four directions.
If fresh remain after BFS completes, return -1.
word-break: DP: canBreak[i] means s[0..i) is segmentable using dictionary words.
Try every word from dictionary as suffix ending at i.
Memoization on substring also works but may be slower.
task-scheduler: Count the most frequent task; it drives minimum idle slots between batches.
Arrange the max frequency block first, then fill gaps.
Formula uses counts and cooldown n; also consider greedy simulation.
trapping-rain-water: Two pointers from left and right; track max left and max right heights.
Water at a position is limited by the shorter side of the two maxes.
Move the pointer with the smaller max inward.
merge-k-sorted-lists: Min-heap of (value, list index, node) or divide-and-conquer pairwise merge.
Compare k heads at each step with a heap for O(n log k) time.
Repeated merge of two lists works but can be less efficient.
word-search-ii: Build a trie from words; DFS from each cell, prune when prefix not in trie.
Mark cells visited during DFS, backtrack after.
Remove words from trie when found to avoid duplicate work.
median-of-two-sorted-arrays: Binary search the partition in the shorter array so left halves have equal total length.
Ensure max of left halves is less than or equal to min of right halves.
Handle odd total length by taking max of left or min of right halves.
longest-valid-parentheses: Stack stores indices; push -1 as base for length calculation.
On ')', pop and compute length if stack non-empty, else push current index.
DP: dp[i] length ending at i also works.
minimum-window-substring: Sliding window with two pointers; expand until valid, shrink from left while valid.
Count needed characters vs current window counts.
Track best window when all required frequencies are met.
edit-distance: DP[i][j] = cost to convert first i chars of word1 to first j of word2.
Space can be reduced to two rows.
largest-rectangle-in-histogram: Monotonic stack of indices with increasing heights.
When a shorter bar appears, pop and compute area with popped height as minimum.
Append zero at end to flush the stack.
n-queens: Backtrack row by row; place queen if column and diagonals are free.
Track occupied columns and two diagonal directions.
Try each column in the current row and recurse.
maximum-profit-in-job-scheduling: Sort jobs by end time; binary search previous non-overlapping job.
DP[i] = max profit using first i jobs: skip or take job i.
Taking job i adds its profit to DP at the last compatible index.
serialize-and-deserialize-binary-tree: Preorder with null markers for missing children, joined by delimiter.
Or level-order BFS with queue and nulls for absent nodes.
Deserialize rebuilds tree using the same traversal order.
find-median-from-data-stream: Two heaps: max-heap for lower half, min-heap for upper half.
Keep sizes balanced so median is top of larger heap or average of both tops.
Insert pushes into appropriate heap then rebalances.
valid-anagram: Two strings of different lengths can never be anagrams, so check that first.
Anagrams have exactly the same multiset of letters. How could you compare multisets cheaply?
Keep a count of 26 letters: add one for each letter of s, subtract one for each letter of t, and check every count ends at zero.
reverse-linked-list: Walk the list once, keeping track of the node you came from.
Before you redirect a node's next pointer, save where it used to point or you will lose the rest of the list.
Three pointers are enough: previous, current and next. When current runs off the end, previous is the new head.
maximum-depth-of-binary-tree: The depth of a tree can be defined in terms of the depths of its two subtrees.
An empty subtree contributes depth 0; a node adds one level on top of its deeper child.
Alternatively, count levels with a breadth-first traversal that processes one whole level per iteration.
same-tree: Compare the two roots first: both missing, exactly one missing, or both present.
If both roots exist and hold equal values, the trees are the same only if both pairs of subtrees are the same.
A recursive check on (p.left, q.left) and (p.right, q.right) covers every node exactly once.
symmetric-tree: A tree is symmetric when its left subtree is a mirror image of its right subtree.
Two subtrees mirror each other when their roots match, the outer children mirror each other, and the inner children mirror each other.
Write a helper that takes two nodes at once, or use a queue that holds nodes in mirrored pairs.
binary-search: Because the array is sorted, one comparison against the middle element rules out half of the remaining range.
Keep two bounds, lo and hi, describing where target could still be.
Compute the middle index as lo + (hi - lo) / 2 and stop when the range becomes empty.
ransom-note: Only the number of each letter matters, not the order.
Count how many of each letter the magazine offers.
Walk the note and spend one count per letter; if any count would drop below zero, the note cannot be built.
majority-element: A hash map of counts works in linear time, but uses linear extra space.
If you sort the array, which index is guaranteed to hold the majority value?
For O(1) space, pair off different values and cancel them: keep a candidate and a counter, incrementing on a match and decrementing otherwise.
single-number: A set or map solves it in linear time, but not in constant space.
Think about a binary operation where combining a value with itself cancels out.
XOR has exactly that property, and it is commutative, so XOR-ing the whole array leaves only the single value.
move-zeroes: Picture writing the non-zero values into a new array in order, then padding with zeros. Can you do that without the new array?
Keep a write index for where the next non-zero value belongs.
After every non-zero value has been written forward, fill the positions from the write index to the end with zeros (or swap as you go).
palindrome-number: Negative numbers, and positive numbers ending in 0, can be rejected immediately.
Reversing the whole number can overflow. What if you only reverse half of it?
Pop digits off the end of x onto a reversed number until the reversed number is at least as large as what remains, then compare the two halves.
roman-to-integer: Map each of the seven symbols to its value.
A symbol is subtracted exactly when the symbol after it has a larger value.
Scan left to right: subtract the current value if the next one is bigger, otherwise add it.
longest-common-prefix: The answer can never be longer than the shortest string.
Compare the strings column by column: position 0 in every string, then position 1, and so on.
Stop at the first column where some string has ended or disagrees with the first string.
plus-one: Adding one only changes the trailing run of 9s and the digit just before it.
Walk from the last digit: a digit below 9 is incremented and you are done; a 9 becomes 0 and the carry moves left.
If the carry survives past the first digit, the result is one digit longer: a 1 followed by zeros.
sqrtx: The answer is the largest integer r such that r * r <= x.
That condition is monotonic in r, so you can binary search over r.
Use 64-bit arithmetic for r * r, since the square of a candidate near 46341 overflows a 32-bit integer.
merge-sorted-array: Merging from the front would overwrite values in nums1 that you still need.
The free space is at the back of nums1, so fill the result from the back.
Compare the largest remaining element of each array and place the larger one at the current write position; once nums2 is exhausted, the rest of nums1 is already in place.
pascals-triangle: The first and last entries of every row are 1.
Each interior entry j of row i equals row[i-1][j-1] + row[i-1][j], so build the rows in order.
diameter-of-binary-tree: Every path has a single highest node where it turns around.
The longest path that turns at a node is the height of its left subtree plus the height of its right subtree.
Compute heights bottom-up in one traversal and record the best left + right sum seen at any node.
balanced-binary-tree: Checking the height difference at the root alone is not enough; every node must satisfy it.
Recomputing heights separately at each node is O(n^2) on a skewed tree.
Return the height from a bottom-up traversal, and use a sentinel such as -1 to report that a subtree is already unbalanced.
middle-of-the-linked-list: Counting the nodes first and then walking half way works in two passes.
Can you find the middle in a single pass?
Move one pointer one step and another two steps at a time; when the fast pointer reaches the end, the slow one is at the middle.
palindrome-linked-list: Copying the values into an array makes the comparison easy, at the cost of O(n) space.
For O(1) space, find the middle of the list with a slow and a fast pointer.
Reverse the second half in place, then walk both halves together comparing values.
intersection-of-two-arrays: Duplicates inside either array do not matter; only which distinct values are present.
Put the values of one array into a set.
Walk the other array and keep each value that is in the set, removing it from the set so it is not added twice.
happy-number: Try a few numbers by hand. The sequence either reaches 1 or starts repeating.
Detecting a repeat is enough: remember every number you have seen in a set.
To avoid the set, run a slow and a fast sequence (Floyd's cycle detection) and stop when they meet or the fast one reaches 1.
is-subsequence: Matching characters of s as early as possible in t is never worse than matching them later.
Keep one index into s and one into t.
Advance through t, and advance the index into s whenever the characters match; s is a subsequence if that index reaches the end.
counting-bits: Counting the bits of every number independently costs O(n log n).
Shifting i right by one drops its lowest bit; you have already computed the answer for that smaller number.
fizz-buzz: Loop i from 1 to n and decide each entry independently.
Check divisibility by 15 (both 3 and 5) before checking 3 or 5 alone.
Alternatively, build the string by appending "Fizz" and "Buzz" separately, and fall back to the number when nothing was appended.
search-insert-position: Both cases ask for the same thing: the first index whose value is at least target.
Binary search over the range [0, n], where n means "after every element".
If nums[mid] < target the answer is to the right of mid; otherwise mid itself may be the answer.
add-binary: The strings can be far longer than any built-in integer type, so add them digit by digit.
Start from the rightmost digit of each string and carry into the next position, exactly as in decimal addition.
Continue while either string has digits left or the carry is non-zero, then reverse the collected digits.
binary-tree-inorder-traversal: Recursion follows the definition directly: left, node, right.
To iterate, simulate the call stack with an explicit stack of nodes.
Push nodes while walking left; when you cannot go further, pop a node, record it, and move to its right child.
flood-fill: Record the starting pixel's original colour before changing anything.
If the new colour equals the original colour there is nothing to do, and filling anyway would loop forever.
Visit connected pixels with DFS or BFS, recolouring each one as you reach it so it is never visited twice.
island-perimeter: Each land cell contributes 4 edges before accounting for its neighbours.
Every pair of adjacent land cells hides two edges, one from each cell.
Count land cells and adjacent land pairs (checking only right and down avoids double counting): perimeter = 4 * land - 2 * pairs.
